Ties to $LMT $RTX $LHX $GD $IRDM $ASTS $NOK $SPCX $BA  Most investors still think Viasat is just satellite internet.  It’s becoming something much bigger.  A vertically integrated defense communications company with recurring government contracts, expanding aviation connectivity, terabit-class satellites, and one of the world’s most valuable spectrum portfolios.  The numbers are starting to tell that story.  • FY2026 record revenue: $4.6B • Record backlog: $4.1B (+15% YoY) • FY2026 awards: $4.9B • Defense backlog +23% YoY • Q4 Defense revenue +12% YoY • Book-to-bill above 1.1x • Positive free cash flow despite peak satellite CapEx • Targeting continued deleveraging through FY2027  The biggest catalyst?  The U.S. Space Force selected Viasat for the Protected Tactical SATCOM-Global (PTS-G) program.  This isn’t just another contract.  It’s part of an IDIQ program worth up to $4B supporting anti-jam X/Ka-band military communications through satellite production, launches, operations, cyber security, and long-term sustainment.  Exactly the type of recurring government revenue Wall Street assigns premium multiples to.  The defense opportunity keeps growing.  Global defense SATCOM is projected to expand from roughly $6B today toward $10B+ over the next decade as geopolitical tensions, electronic warfare, AI-enabled battlefields, and resilient communications become national priorities.  Viasat sits directly in that niche alongside names like $LHX $RTX $GD and $LMT while also competing with $IRDM across government communications.  ViaSat-3 may be the biggest long-term catalyst.  Three next-generation GEO satellites will increase global network capacity by multiple terabits per second.  That unlocks thousands of additional aircraft, ships, government users, and enterprise customers without requiring the same level of infrastructure investment.  Higher utilization.  Higher margins.  Higher recurring revenue.  The aviation segment continues quietly compounding.  • 1,000+ connected aircraft • Expanding commercial airline partnerships • Cockpit connectivity • Fuel efficiency software • In-flight advertising monetization  Another overlooked catalyst…  Industry consolidation.  Following $RKLB Rocket Lab’s acquisition of $IRDM Iridium, analysts began calling Viasat one of the last major independent global satellite spectrum assets.  Spectrum scarcity matters.  As defense spending accelerates and governments seek secure communications infrastructure, strategic satellite assets become increasingly valuable.  Analysts continue carrying price targets around $90-$100+, with several even higher following recent defense wins.  But the fundamentals continue improving.  This isn’t simply a satellite company anymore.  It’s becoming a critical communications infrastructure company sitting at the intersection of defense, aerospace, aviation, cybersecurity, AI, and global connectivity.  One worth keeping on the radar after this pullback.

$RKLB / $SPCX / $LMT  Rocket Lab, Lockheed Martin among the partners in SpaceX's military space-laser project  By Christine Ji  (MarketWatch) - Government documents show a lineup of defense contractors joining SpaceX to create a satellite network to track airborne threats  The U.S. government is tapping both of the country's biggest launch providers, Rocket Lab and SpaceX, for its Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program.  Rocket Lab, Lockheed Martin and L3 Harris Technologies are among a group of eight aerospace and defense companies sharing a multibillion-dollar military vendor pool with SpaceX for a new space defense program, government documents show.  Last month, Space Systems Command - an organization under the U.S. Space Force - announced that it had awarded SpaceX (SPCX) a $4.16 billion contract for the Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program. The Space Force, a branch of the U.S. Armed Forces under the Department of the Air Force, had previously indicated that there were a total of nine vendors in the pool. According to government records posted on the federal government's procurement portal managed by the General Services Administration, Rocket Lab, York Space Systems, Visto 360 AI, Wildstar and Systems & Technology Research received contracts valued at $10,000 each under the SB-AMTI initiative. The records were first flagged on social media by space investor Jacob Keeton and a user of the social-media platform X posting under the handle @ trypto_tran.  Government records also showed that Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin and L3 Harris received contracts for $6,666 each under the SB-AMTI initiative. All nine SB-AMTI contracts were signed between March 23 and March 25 of this year and run until March 2031.  A Space Force spokesperson told MarketWatch that Space Systems Command could neither confirm nor deny the vendor identities due to national-security interests.  Representatives for SpaceX, Rocket Lab, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, L3Harris Technologies, Systems & Technology Research, Wildstar and Visto 360 AI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from MarketWatch.   York Space Systems said that it could not confirm or deny any information about the contract posted on the government website.  SpaceX's contract shows that the ultimate scope of the SB-AMTI program - which aims to implement a space-based sensing layer to track and target airborne threats - extends far beyond the Pentagon's initial $4.16 billion disclosure.   SpaceX secured $2.637 billion in total obligations in March, with the agreement's maximum potential contract value capping at $9.34 billion. The other eight vendors' total obligations of $10,000 and $6,666 are placeholder allocations designed to grant them a position in the vendor pool.  Traditionally, the U.S. military has tracked airborne threats, such as missiles and drones, by flying aircraft over areas of interest. However, the rapid proliferation of advanced antiaircraft missiles by foreign adversaries has diminished the effectiveness of this strategy.  This SB-AMTI award is projected to deploy a constellation of satellites in low-Earth orbit by 2028 to continuously monitor global airspace and eliminate operational blind spots. Satellites with advanced sensors will sweep through airspace to pick up information that traditional airborne radars can't read, then beam the data through a laser-linked orbital mesh network directly to meet warfighter needs.  SpaceX and Rocket Lab are the two biggest launch-services providers in the U.S., and also provide end-to-end satellite manufacturing services.  In the May announcement, Space System Command shared that "Space Force anticipates issuing multiple awards in the coming year to drive a vendor-diverse expansion" - a signal that the nine-vendor pool anchored by SpaceX is only the beginning of a larger pipeline.  -Christine Ji  (END) Dow Jones Newswires  https://t.co/90XfftvkrX

JUST IN: NASA and Lockheed Martin $LMT are preparing to test robotic welding in space, potentially enabling the construction of massive structures in orbit that are too large to fit inside conventional rockets.  The experiment, called JOINS, is scheduled to launch to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman's Cygnus XL spacecraft later this month.  Once aboard the ISS, robotic equipment will attempt to weld aluminum and stainless steel using two different techniques:  (1) Laser welding, which melts and fuses metal using a concentrated beam of light.  (2) Friction stir welding, which joins metals using a rotating tool without melting them.  The experiment is scheduled for March 2027, with cameras monitoring the process and welded samples returning to Earth for analysis.  If successful, the technology could help enable the construction of larger satellite antennas, solar arrays, space stations and other orbital infrastructure without being constrained by rocket payload dimensions.  The goal is to eventually build and repair large structures directly in space rather than launching them fully assembled from Earth.

Karman Holdings ($KRMN) is one of the most overlooked “pick-and-shovel” plays in aerospace and defense. Instead of building rockets, it supplies the mission-critical payload protection, aerodynamic interstage, propulsion, and launch systems that many of the industry’s biggest names rely on.  The company supports 130+ programs across 80+ customers, with ties to $RKLB, $LMT, $NOC, $BA, $RTX, ULA’s Vulcan, Blue Origin’s New Glenn, NASA missions, and numerous hypersonic and missile defense programs. Its top three customers have historically represented roughly 47% of revenue, but no single program accounts for more than ~10% of sales, providing diversified exposure across the ecosystem.  The stock has fallen from over $118 to roughly $50 despite fundamentals continuing to strengthen.  Why?  • Premium valuation reset after trading around 220x earnings. • Q1 revenue of $151.2M (+51% YoY) came in just below lofty expectations. • A 14M-share secondary offering created significant selling pressure, with proceeds going to existing shareholders rather than the company. • Broader aerospace and defense names pulled back after massive runs.  Meanwhile, the business kept improving.  • FY2025 revenue grew roughly 37% YoY. • Q1 revenue grew another 51% YoY. • Gross profit reached a record ~$64M with gross margins around 40%. • Adjusted EBITDA climbed to ~$45M. • Funded backlog expanded from $758M to $801M before surpassing $1B, up 61% YoY. • Active pipeline tripled from roughly $1B to approximately $3B. • Management raised 2026 guidance to $720-735M revenue, implying roughly 54-56% annual growth, with adjusted EBITDA of $208.5-219.5M. • Around 90% of 2026 revenue guidance was already supported by backlog and existing awards.  The niche is where the story gets interesting.  Space & Launch represents roughly one-third of revenue (~34%) and continues benefiting from rising commercial and national security launch cadence. The segment generated $43.9M during Q1, growing 29.5% YoY as launch activity accelerated.  Hypersonics & Strategic Missile Defense continues seeing strong demand as the U.S. ramps production of THAAD, PAC-3, Standard Missile, PrSM, and other next-generation defense systems.  Tactical Missiles, Integrated Defense, Maritime Defense, UAS launchers, counter-UAS, propulsion systems, payload protection, and advanced composites all add additional growth vectors.  Global launches continue setting records, with roughly 315 successful orbital launches during 2025, up approximately 24% YoY, while the U.S. accounted for around 61% of those launches. More launches generally mean more demand for qualified suppliers like Karman.  Unlike launch providers, Karman doesn’t have to pick the winning rocket.  It simply supplies critical hardware across multiple winners.  The company estimates roughly a $60B addressable market spanning space, hypersonics, missile defense, and tactical systems, yet generates under $1B in annual revenue today, implying well under 2% penetration with significant room to expand. After having some time to digest the NGSRI news  • Sam was oozing confidence about the $LPTH / $LMT product as recently as a widely disseminated video interview 2 weeks ago.  • If a vendor can come and knock out in <8 months (Sep 26-May 27) what $RTX and $LMT have been working on for 3 years hats off to them.  But even THEN the DOW wants multiple vendors in their programs to get away from the last X decades of relying on sole vendors.   • Any technology solution in the next <8 months surely won't be an "off the shelf" solution.  • A theory exists that $RTX is doing so poorly, the DOW wants another vendor competing with $LMT "down the line" as $RTX gets pushed out.  That would be an uber bullish viewing but I try not to drink the Kool Aid.  But I would be tickled if this is the outcome.  • While we like to think $LPTH as our little undiscovered baby, there have been some big accounts who have glommed onto the story in the past 1-4 months which have brought a lot of attention to the name.  In retrospect more than I realized.  These accounts bring "hot money" but often not "lasting money" - many of their followers want near instant results or they are gone.  Fair play - that comes with more attention.  The price reaction function yesterday makes clear to me that this isn't the little quiet name very few know about, as it was in Sept 2025 when some of us first got into the story.   • The only thing that would change my thesis about NGSRI specific is the Army pushing out the date when they want vendors to start delivering product, which at this point remains fiscal 2028.  That begins Oct 1, 2027 and ends Sep 30, 2028.   Buying 11,000 missiles in that time frame means a company needs to be in FRIP (full rate production) by winter 27-28 at the latest - preferably earlier.  Reverse engineering means LRIP (low rate production) by next summer at the latest - preferably earlier but after this announcement it won't be earlier.  Hence if we see a notice the ENTIRE program has been pushed out a year to Fiscal Year 2029 that would be the time to ask serious questions. We are not there.  • Some have said this action was well known to management in advance - if so my only qualm in this situation is that this sort of information should have been publicly messaged to the market because it obviously caught the masses by surprise.  The market takes "bad news" better than "uncertainty".  Maybe a small lesson for a management which until 6 months ago had almost zero attention on it.  And now has many more eyes on it.  Expectation setting matters.  • This management is more about putting their head down & growing the business and not as much about optics (pun intended).  They don't provide guidance, they now are only announcing large contracts and shunning press releases of any smaller orders, have a less frequent interview cadence then similar sized companies, etc.  I don't see those things changing however I do think it was a misstep to at some point in the last 6 months not tell the investor base "understand it is typical for the Army to open up the competition one last time in the closing moments" (or however it needs to be said more accurately).  For example Allan at $UMAC has told us in advance the company will need to change auditors as it nears a $100M annual revenue run rate because SOX compliance comes into frame and their current auditor doesn't offer that.  An auditor change often leads to panic in the retail investor base and PPS reduction because people think the current auditor found something unbecoming and management is getting rid of the dirty laundry.  So this has been telegraphed in advance at $UMAC ; hence this event at $LPTH  - if known by management in advance - would have been nice to have been telegraphed in advance.  • I am segregating the 2 new items - (a) new competitors invited ("pretty standard these days") and (b) timeline pushed out from fall 2026 to spring 2027.  Management most likely was not aware of the latter so no communication expected on that front; but communication on the former would have been helpful.  • Everything else remains intact including executive orders, anti Chinese supply chain movement, germanium price increases, Chinese hoarding of germanium, and design plans (often for 10+ year programs) that seek non germanium solutions. One of the dirty little secrets of investing is this:  Virtually every huge long-term winner had periods when the stock did nothing:  - $MCD was flat from 1996 through 2005 - So was $MSFT from 2000 through 2015 - Ditto for $WMT between 2008 and 2015 - And $RY.TO from 2017 - 2021  There are hundreds of other examples, too.  You're going to think this is a #neversell post, but it isn't. I can understand why someone would get frustrated and sell if a stock is dead money for the better part of a decade. That's a long time!  What I've found is the middle of these prolonged slumps are terrific buying opportunities. Valuations are compressed because investors think current temporary problems are permanent. They give us dividend investors both increased income today and the potential for nice capital gains in the future. It might not happen for a year or two, but long-term we usually get rewarded.   Obviously, identifying the difference between temporary problems and structural changes in the business is not easy. I've certainly gotten some wrong. But the winners often more than make up for the losers.   In my view it's generally a good strategy because:  1. Good companies with histories of long-term success didn't get there by accident. Kind of like the Lindy Effect 2. You can buy these assets at a discount, which obviously helps 3. The dividend received while waiting is much higher than normal  I find these companies in a few different ways, including:  1. Look for disconnect between the long-term business performance and the share price 1a. Flat earnings for a year or three is an excellent indicator. Sometimes companies overearn (like retail/CPG companies during COVID) and need a bit of a cooling off period after 2. Compare the current valuation to the valuation in the past. Same with the dividend yield. Opportunities jump out, plus you don't get anchored to a certain valuation or a certain yield 3. Look at investor sentiment on here. I want to see lots of bearishness. A *lot* of investors will see a falling share price and invent narratives.   We are told that a stock price will follow its earnings. That generally tends to happen over the long-term, but all sorts of weird stuff happens in the short-term. That's the fertile hunting ground, and most will struggle to go there because we've been conditioned to think falling share price = bad company.

🍟 Dividend King $MCD hit a 52-week low this week and I've seen some folks seemingly throw their hands up in despair. That caught me by surprise, considering I own McDonald's and haven't felt an ounce of pressure during this sell-off.  "Buy right and sit tight" allows an investor a lot of grace, and depressurizes the emotion that all of us contend with.  I'd have to believe those who are panicking about a steady Blue Chip like MCD are those who paid too dear a price when stock sentiment was high, as opposed to those who bought at more appropriate valuations, when the market was more pessimistic about its future.  I bought MCD over a decade ago. Some people have called it the world's best Real Estate play (due to their high-margin franchising model).  But I've seen many challenges its gone through along the way, to put shareholders in a foul mood. There was a time that people thought it was an "also-ran" and there was no more growth left because of dirty bathrooms and dingy interiors. There was a time that people thought their menu was too extensive. There was a time when people feared that healthier eating habits would steer away typical fans of fries/burgers. There's been times when people demanded that they offer their breakfast/lunch/dinner menus during all hours. There's been times when people were mad about removing Play Places and installing Kiosk ordering screens in the restaurants. There's been times when people thought they couldn't withstand the pressure of being forced to sell all their Russian operations on the cheap. There's been times when people are nervous about the revolving door in the C-suite. There's been times when people are angry over broken ice cream machines. There's been times when people thought all restaurants should offer McCafes and be open 24/7. Currently, there's nerves over GLP-1 drugs and inflation. And that won't be the end of it. There will be future challenges as well, as there are for all businesses. More times than not, temporary challenges for Blue Chip companies are exactly what a potential long term investor should be hoping for (assuming the challenges can be overcome eventually).  As for me, I'm staying put in my shares. And if a gun was held to my head and I was forced to take action on MCD here, I'd be much closer to being a buyer of the shares, rather than a seller. My Dividend Stairstep chart shows a reasonable entry just below $260 (using  Dividend Yield Theory that I teach in my DGI classes at @MarketScholars ).  One interesting thing about my personal position (my wife actually has a lower cost basis than me) is that the numbers are currently nice and round (doubles, triples, etc.) to provide an educational example of the power of Dividend Reinvestment.  The problem is that a lot of people give up on DRIP way too soon because they can't see a meaningful difference of implementing it in the short-term. But I'm here to tell you that it makes a substantial difference if you're able to hold stocks for a decade or more under that program.  It somewhat reminds me of the phrase: "The chains of habit are too weak to be felt until they are too strong to be broken."  In my case, I put appx $10,000 of outside money into MCD. Despite the stock being at a 52-week low, my position is now worth just over $30,000 (green rectangle). The reason my brokerage statement shows a cost basis of $15,000 in the red rectangle (as opposed to my $10K outside money figure) is due to quarterly Dividend Reinvestment. In other words, the true amount of money I've reinvested into the shares is 50% more, even though I didn't have to physically put in any extra outside money myself. I simply had to delay gratification by not spending my dividend cash on frivolous things like fast-food burgers & fries (although I did a fair bit of that nonetheless 😉), and instead, instruct my broker to reinvest those cash dividends back into the same quality business four times per year.  Automated & easy.  So, my brokerage statement will tell me I have a double (purple rectangle with $15K turning into $30K). But in my own head I think of it as a triple (my outside money of $10K turning into $30K of current value). The extra 100% of returns is due entirely to complimentary Dividend Reinvestment available through most reputable online brokerages, and a insistence of not interrupting it along the way.  This post is not meant to be a suggestion for anyone to buy MCD (I'm not your advisor). But I'm hoping it can provide a friendly reminder of the power of investing in solid Blue Chip dividend growth stocks at reasonable prices, and allowing time to do the heavy lifting through quarterly compounding.

I'm still digesting that McDonald's call, which was something. $MCD   First: Chris Kempczinski and McDonald's should get some real credit for their candor. A lot of companies (hint: Yum Brands) are way too focused on the positive while blowing off serious problems. (hint: Pizza Hut)  But there are some real implications to the company's quarter and they're not insignificant.  McDonald's franchisees agreed, with considerable cajoling, to lower prices and offer more discounts. The result last quarter was less traffic, despite a bunch of marketing promotions, including beverages, which did better than expected. Not even the World Cup helped.  When more discounts result in less traffic, it means that existing restaurant customers are buying cheaper, less profitable food, but there are fewer of them. So the profitability is much worse. (Oh, and beef costs are soaring right now, which obviously makes matters worse.)  So your average franchisee makes a lot less money now than they did a year ago or a few months ago.  McDonald's is about to start asking franchisees to remodel their restaurants again as part of their 10-year remodel cycle. That's a key part of the company's "Next" plan.   But franchisees will have less cashflow and will be less able to afford the cost to remodel those locations. And McDonald's expended considerable political capital to convince franchisees to do those discounts. They did not work.  Suffice it to say, the company has some real work to do. And so that probably explains the change in U.S. leadership and Chris K's candor. But I probably won't forget that call anytime soon.

What if $MCD were a REIT? 🍟  The former real estate developer and Wall Street writer in me couldn’t resist a little back-of-the-napkin math.  In 2025, $MCD collected approximately $10.44 BILLION in franchise rent (separate from its royalty income).  Now imagine placing its owned properties and leasehold interests into a hypothetical “Golden Arches REIT.”  For this exercise, assume:  • $8 billion in annual property-level net operating income.  • $25 billion of net debt assigned to the REIT.  • Approximately 711 million shares, equivalent to $MCD’s year-end share count.  The $8 billion is a modeling assumption, not reported REIT earnings. The debt allocation is hypothetical, too.  What might investors pay?  👉At an 8% cap rate: $100 billion property-business value → approximately $106 per share after debt.  👉At a 7% cap rate: $114 billion value → approximately $126 per share.  👉At a 6% cap rate: $133 billion value → approximately $152 per share.  That’s a hypothetical $106–$152 per share attributable to the rental business, excluding the separate value of royalties and restaurant operations.  ($MCD closed at $237.02 using my hypothetical $126-per-share valuation for “Golden Arches REIT,” leaving roughly $111 per share for the operating and royalty business).   But there’s a catch: $MCD’s doesn’t own every site; some rental income comes from subleases, and the rent stream is closely tied to the strength of the brand and franchisees (however, a REIT can hold owned real estate or qualifying leasehold interests, so leasing properties would not, by itself, prevent this hypothetical company from qualifying as a REIT.)  There’s also a tax wrinkle: Congress generally closed the tax-free REIT spinoff loophole through the PATH Act of 2015. Subject to limited exceptions, a corporation can no longer spin its real estate into a REIT tax-free.  So this is a valuation thought experiment, not a proposal for a tax-free transaction. Actual trading value would depend on overhead, capital spending, growth, lease terms, and how much debt the REIT inherited.  Still, it’s a fascinating "back of the napkin" exercise. SBUX may still be on an old MSFT perpetual license, perhaps AX or perhaps Great Plains which is being sunset in 2029, or perhaps they built a custom app on Azure.   If they are replacing 1 custom app with another one, its a net-neutral to MSFT. If they replace an old perpetual license with a new modern app on Azure, its a net positive to MSFT.   Migrating off old systems is a tale as old as time in IT. And in horizontal categories like inventory mgmt, warehouse mgmt, for Fortune 500 companies, internally-built systems will always be on the table to consider bc few SaaS apps can scale to that degree and serve all the particular needs of a customer that size (why $TOST is an SMB product).   Personally, I dont see this as evidence of disruption.

Thesis 1: Starbucks’ Store Closures Artificially Inflate SSSG More Than Management Has Disclosed.  Evidence: We mapped all 584 closed U.S. stores using opening and closing data from https://t.co/PbGyDRoB0D and additional scrapes. Utilizing geospatial satellite imagery analysis, we measured their proximity to surviving Starbucks locations. 62% of closed stores had a company-operated Starbucks shop within 1 mile, vs. 26% of remaining open stores. To determine whether Starbucks disproportionately closed stores in weaker trade areas, we matched the closed shops with 584 randomly selected open stores in equally dense trade areas and compared AUV drivers (# of schools, hotels, office buildings, colleges, etc.) and competitor density using the same geospatial satellite imagery analysis. Counterintuitively, closed shops were located in more attractive trade areas, averaging 128.7 AUV drivers within one mile vs. 107.3 for open stores, while competitor density was effectively unchanged at 44.1 vs. 43.4. The ~250 additional stores announced for closure in Q4 show the same pattern: 52 vs. 43.1 AUV drivers and 34.1 vs. 31.7 competitors, with 56% of stores having a sister within 1 mile. This closure pattern is consistent with Starbucks disproportionately closing stores where demand can be transferred to nearby locations. We corroborated this with interviews across 300 stores: 89% of stores within 0.25 miles of a closure reported becoming “noticeably busier” in September 2025, with traffic up ~27% by employee estimates, and 82% of the Starbucks partners attributed the increase to a nearby Starbucks closure without being prompted. By contrast, only 7% of control stores reported becoming busier, and none cited closures. Our 1.2M store-week database shows that the company-operated stores within one mile of the 2025 closures exhibited a ~6.4-hour-per-week lift y/y vs. ~2.1 for other North American CO shops, consistent with their absorbing the influx of traffic. Interestingly, 63% of stores reported the traffic bump has since faded, suggesting this was a one-time transfer rather than an improvement in underlying demand, which Starbucks will begin lapping next quarter. Based on our survey and third-party estimates, we estimate retention was trending at >90%. This is also in line with traffic growth estimates we heard from store managers in our 300+ calls. Using the average closed store AUV, closures, and customer retention, we estimate ~$1.03bn of annual revenue was transferred to surviving stores, equivalent to ~425 bps of inorganic comp growth. Evidence: Using emerging brand store-opening data, construction filings, and 80,777 scraped Google reviews to estimate opening dates, we tracked changes in emerging-brand density around Starbucks locations from 2023 to September 2026. We found that the share of Starbucks company-operated shops that have an emerging brand within a mile has nearly doubled from 8.5% (2023) to 16.3% (Sept. 2026). This expansion is largely incremental to existing coffee shop supply: only 8.3% of units built within the last year replaced another coffee shop, suggesting most new units are adding competition for Starbucks rather than replacing incumbents. We analyzed 191 Texas construction filings for new 7 Brew locations and found that 73% of the 191 next-cohort 7 Brew locations are located within a mile of a Starbucks drive-thru. Former 7 Brew regional managers indicate this is deliberate, citing Starbucks trade areas as attractive locations because of the opportunity to “steal their customers.” Emerging brands’ encroachment coincides with substantial share loss. Our credit card alternative data across 150M consumers shows Starbucks’ share of tracked spend across Starbucks, $BROS, and 7 Brew falling from 83.2% to 66.4% since January 2022, while Dutch Bros increased from 16.7% to 25.3% and 7 Brew from 0.1% to 8.2%. Separately, our foot traffic data shows that when a Dutch Bros or 7 Brew opens within one mile of a Starbucks, traffic at the Starbucks location declines 8-10% on average, providing direct evidence that these brands are substituting for Starbucks. The competitive threat is also expanding beyond Starbucks’ drive-thrus. Channel checks with six Albertsons managers found that Dutch Bros’ newly introduced CPG products have been selling out within weeks and outperforming existing Starbucks offerings. Meanwhile, Dutch, a traditionally suburban only chain, has recently opened its first urban store with a fully walk-up format. This has been one of their best performing locations over the last quarters, with our interviews with Broistas during our site visit in Los Angeles revealing the format’s higher order-ahead mix allows the location to deliver higher throughput than suburban locations. The company’s intensifying landscape is pushing Starbucks toward a more complex menu, given the customizability appeal of the share-stealing emerging brands, leading to overworked employees who are becoming increasingly negative about the brand. Starbucks is attempting to deliver a faster, more service-intensive experience while simultaneously operating with fewer employees per store than emerging competitors: Dutch Bros averages 27.3 employees/store despite ~33% lower average square footage per company-operated shop. We believe Starbucks’ expanding menu and higher service standards make its FY2025 staffing level unsustainable, requiring continued labor investment rather than the normalization that the Street models. Morgan Stanley Downgrades $CMG to Equalweight from Overweight, Lowers PT to $37 from $49  Analyst comments: "We are stepping aside on CMG and downgrading to Equalweight. We do not have conviction the narrative changes quickly here, and we trim both our numbers and our target multiple. Our prior Overweight view, which has not borne out of late, was based on structural tailwinds, new sales drivers after a slow 2025, leading unit growth, margin recovery, and tech benefits. Most of these have underwhelmed versus our expectations, and while sales are improving, we are not calling for beats versus consensus on a sustained basis.  We see less valuation downside, but in downgrading, we are largely agreeing with what seems to be the dominant investor view: CMG likely faces a future of more modest comps and margin expansion, unit growth could wisely be trimmed, and 25-30x, which it is now below, seems like the right multiple range for a company growing earnings probably ~15% in a good year. For the 7th largest U.S. QSR, this is still good, but the headiest growth years seem less likely to repeat.  We do not expect CMG to miss the 2Q, but mark down forward earnings ~4% here and use a lower multiple than prior. CMG remains on-trend; it is not a structural loser, and it is something we would look to recommend again, but this does seem like a new phase of its lifecycle."  Analyst: Brian Harbour

$PLTR IS BECOMING INFRASTRUCTURE FOR THE FOOD SYSTEM  Palantir working with $CMG matters less because of the size of one contract and more because it shows the commercial playbook working in another vertical. Palantir starts with a high stakes workflow like food safety, builds that into Foundry, then has a path into inventory, procurement, labor and other operating decisions. That is already how it has expanded across Tyson, General Mills and Wendy’s purchasing network.  For Chipotle the value proposition is unusually clear because food safety has historically been one of the biggest risks to the brand. Its new platform appears to combine health inspection scores, pest incidents and employee illness data into a store level risk score that could help management catch problems earlier. Restaurant level margin also fell to 25.2% from 27.4% last quarter, so avoiding even one major outbreak could justify years of software spend while protecting traffic and the brand at the same time.  The part I find more interesting is how repeatable this model is becoming. Palantir finished Q2 with $6.238B of U.S. commercial remaining deal value, up 124%, while U.S. commercial TCV reached a record $2.132B. Chipotle adds another recognizable consumer brand to that reference list, and every successful deployment makes it easier to sell the same operating layer into the next company.  There are limits because a store level dashboard cannot stop every food safety problem and supplier contamination still requires traceability and fast action. That is what makes the bigger thesis more interesting though. If Palantir can connect food safety, supply chain and operating data across restaurants and suppliers, then Foundry starts looking less like another analytics tool and more like infrastructure for how the food system actually runs. The Chipotle contract itself is financially immaterial, but as another proof point for that commercial expansion story I think it matters.

$SBUX $CMG merger offers the wrong kind of synergy.  The overlap between the two brands is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium.  The Financial Times October 9, 2026  Putting the band back together is surely a great feeling, but a dubious corporate strategy. Starbucks chief Brian Niccol has considered a merger with Chipotle, his $41bn rival — and former employer — the FT reported on Thursday. However neat the match might seem from Starbucks’ corner office, it makes little sense for shareholders.  Niccol knows Chipotle very well indeed. He ran the Mexican-themed restaurant chain for six years before decamping in 2024 to the world’s biggest coffee chain, which was then in a state of considerable disarray. Seen from afar, the two do faintly similar things, serving comestibles to customers who are in a hurry. Both have large, sometimes restive workforces. Moreover, the ways in which they differ might seem from a distance like opportunities. Chipotle’s balance sheet is free of debt; gearing it up a little could provide low-hanging fruit. And while Starbucks has a sprawling global network, Chipotle has yet to venture outside the US, apart from a smattering of international stores.   But do these companies really belong together? Not really. For one, the overlap is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium. Imagine Niccol could shave 10 per cent off Chipotle’s food, drink and packaging costs and halve its general overheads. That would save $770mn a year, Lex reckons using Royal Bank of Canada forecasts, giving an after-tax return on investment of just 6 per cent. Anything below 10 per cent should make investors nervous.  More importantly, Niccol hasn’t finished fixing up his present employer, making this a poor time to take on his old one. Starbucks shares have gone sideways since the day his appointment was announced. Profitability isn’t yet where it used to be. Same-store sales growth of 8 per cent in the latest quarter suggests the company has turned a corner, but recent numbers are still flattered by the previous year’s decline.  Chipotle has fared much worse, as has most of the US restaurant sector. But for Niccol to argue he can do a better job than its current leadership might be somewhat problematic, since Chipotle chief Scott Boatwright was his direct report for six years. Conversely, keeping the brand separate and its leaders in place — the Starbucks boss spent more than a decade at multi-brand restaurant group Yum Brands — would further trim the potential cost savings.  Perhaps it’s just that Niccol could use some more motivation. After all, the generous $100mn-plus package he received in 2024, linked to the company’s share price, has mostly failed to pay out. Worse, having started his role in sunny California, he now spends significant time in rainy Seattle. Starbucks should want to keep Niccol engaged, but buying Chipotle is too high a price. john.foley@ft.com

The debt generates recurring interest income.  The equity investments—often 5-50% ownership stakes—create upside that helps fund supplemental dividends.  That’s a powerful combination. Here's how it likely works:  Kentucky Power is a regulated utility. It earns a regulator-approved return on plants once they're running, charged to customers through rates. While a plant is being built, the utility is borrowing and spending but collecting nothing. Normally it books those financing costs as AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction), adds them to the plant's price tag, and customers pay them later.  WULF appears to be covering that cost instead. The exact mechanics aren't disclosed yet: interest only or the utility's full return, paid as incurred or as a lump sum. Our guess, could be $100-300M over the build, depending on structure. AEP gets paid sooner, the plant goes into rates cheaper, and existing customers don't fund a plant built for a data center. Looks to be in line thematically with what the White House has demanded.  This is not behind-the-meter because WULF won't own the plant. It will pay tariff rates like any other customer, plus this carry. Expect it to pass through to the tenant in the lease. The Public Service Commission filing later this year will likely reveal more details.

Why This Metals Cycle Could Be Structural, Not Speculative $GLD $SLV $COPX   Please ❤️like, bookmark🔖, and 🔁share with fellow investors  In this Short video, @JonathanWellum and @AdamTaggart examine why the current metals cycle could be structural rather than simply another speculative boom — and why the long-term case for gold, silver and copper may remain intact despite the recent correction.  *  Precious metals became extremely frothy during last year’s blockbuster run, so some of that excess needed to come out. And it did.   Now the price action appears more constructive, raising the possibility that a meaningful base is forming.  But the bigger argument isn’t about calling the exact bottom. It’s about what the supply-demand picture could look like over the next 3–5 years.  Silver and copper face significant structural deficits while demand remains relatively inelastic and continues to grow.  Both are essential inputs for electrification, infrastructure and the broader technological buildout. If that transformation continues, the world is going to need substantially more of these metals.  *  Copper illustrates the challenge particularly well.  Large new mines can take a decade to discover, permit, finance and develop, meaning supply cannot quickly respond to higher demand.  An estimated $250 billion of additional investment may be needed in copper mining over the coming years.  That combination of constrained supply, long development timelines and rising consumption could provide an unusually strong fundamental floor for prices.  *  There is also a monetary dimension to the metals thesis.  With global debt estimated around 350% of GDP, some degree of inflation or currency debasement may ultimately be part of how that debt burden is managed.   Scarce real assets could therefore benefit not only from physical shortages but also from concerns about the long-term purchasing power of money.  *  Gold has another role entirely.  Central banks continue accumulating it, suggesting gold is becoming increasingly important within the global monetary system.  This doesn’t necessarily imply a return to a gold standard. Instead, it reflects something more fundamental: declining trust.  When countries trust each other less, they want collateral without counterparty risk. Gold remains one of the few globally recognized reserve assets that does not depend on another government’s promise to pay.  *  The obvious counterargument is history.  Gold and silver have experienced vertical, speculative runs before — most notably around 1980 and 2011 — followed by major corrections and long periods of disappointing returns.  Could this be another version of the same story?  The argument against that outcome is that today’s structural fundamentals may be considerably stronger.   Copper and silver aren't merely speculative assets; the global economy physically needs more of them, while new supply is difficult and expensive to develop.  Gold, meanwhile, is being supported by central-bank demand and a changing global monetary landscape.  *  None of this means metals move straight higher. Volatility and significant corrections should be expected.  That’s why the strategy isn’t to chase metals when they're running. It’s to take a disciplined approach, dollar-cost average into high-conviction opportunities and focus on the 3–5 year fundamentals. 9-15-26 Gold Is A Diversifier, Not An Inflation Trade $GLD  Gold has been under pressure lately as higher rates, rising real yields and a stronger dollar weigh on precious metals. But if you’re looking at gold purely as an inflation hedge, you may be looking at it the wrong way.  The better reason to own gold is diversification.  There are very long periods when gold does not outperform inflation. That doesn’t mean gold is broken. Over a long enough timeframe, gold can provide non-correlated exposure relative to stocks and bonds, help offset portfolio volatility and diversify risks that affect traditional financial assets.  The key is matching your expectations to your timeframe.  If you own gold as a 10- or 20-year portfolio diversifier, judging it because inflation is outrunning gold this year misses the point. But if you’re trading gold from one day to the next, forget the long-term diversification argument and trade the price in front of you.  For the shorter-term gold outlook, one of the most important variables to watch is real interest rates. Rising real yields can pressure gold because investors can earn higher inflation-adjusted returns elsewhere. A strengthening dollar can add another headwind.  Another mistake is chasing an asset after a major run. Gold and silver $SLV attracted enormous attention after their recent momentum, leading some investors to dramatically increase their precious-metals exposure. But every asset goes through cycles.  Stocks, bonds, gold, silver, Bitcoin — everything has bull and bear cycles. You can cherry-pick almost any timeframe to make an asset look fantastic or terrible. And if you buy near the peak of one cycle, you may spend the next cycle underperforming.  The same principle applies to stocks. Buying equities at 40x earnings and assuming historical market returns will simply continue ignores the importance of starting valuation and timeframe.  The bigger lesson is about portfolio construction: know why you own an asset.  If gold is there for long-term diversification, don't judge the thesis by what happened this week, this month or even this year. If it's a short-term trade, manage it like a trade.  Gold doesn't have to beat inflation every year to serve a purpose in a portfolio.  Please ❤️like, bookmark🔖, and 🔁share with fellow investors.

$NEM Loss  ~$821k  In a Uniswap V2 style pair such as PancakeSwap's, tokens arriving at the pair do not prove a sale.  Anyone can send tokens to the pair address.  Until someone calls swap(), those tokens are just excess balance above the stored reserves, and skim() lets any caller withdraw that excess to an address of their choice.  Attack flow: 1/send NEM to the pair, which raised pendingLpSellRecycle,  2/call skim() to take most of those tokens back, which did not lower the counter,  3/call flushLpSellRecycle(), which burned NEM that belonged to the pool's liquidity providers, not the attacker's tokens.

"How many confirmations should I wait for?"  Depends on what you're protecting.  A common Bitcoin convention for high-value transfers is 6 confirmations. But $BELLS, $DOGE, and Pepecoin Network's $PEP all target ~1-minute block times - so six confirmations is roughly six minutes at target block time, not an hour. Real block discovery is probabilistic, so the actual wait can be a little faster or slower.  The right number scales with several things at once: how much you're moving, chain security, counterparty risk, block time, and the receiver's own policy. There's no fixed habit that works everywhere.  A practical guide:  → Small payments (a few BELLS, a coffee-sized DOGE transfer) 1–2 confirmations is often reasonable - assuming both sides accept the small reorg / double-spend risk for low-value transfers.  → Marketplace buys, regular transfers, mid-value sends 2–6 confirmations, depending on value and the marketplace's own policy.  → Large transfers, exchange deposits, anything you really can't lose 6+ confirmations as a starting point. Exchange policies vary widely by asset - some credit at 2, some require 14+. Check the receiving service's specific requirement before you assume.  → Inscription transfers Watch for two things: the base-chain transaction confirming, and the inscription appearing at the destination address in the inscription explorer. Ordinal-style assets depend on indexer state, not just UTXO state - and safe sending also depends on the wallet handling input/output ordering correctly.  One confirmation isn't always "enough." Six isn't always overkill.  The risk decides.

Three patterns that show up across thin UTXO inscription markets - Bitcoin Ordinals, Doginals, Bellinals, $PEP L1 inscriptions. Worth knowing on one chain, useful across all of them.  1. The phantom floor  The floor is the lowest active listing. It's a seller's intent to sell - not proof that anyone will pay it.  In thin markets, some floor listings sit unmoved for weeks even when comparable pieces are trading. Others get swept the moment a real buyer shows up. The "real" floor isn't what's listed - it's what's clearing.  Quick check: pull a collection's activity tab. If floor listings get bought when volume picks up, the floor is real. If they sit there even as similar pieces trade, the floor is signaling.  2. The follow-the-listing rule  When a piece clears, the next comparable listing often gets repriced quickly. The first visible sale anchors a new mental price for whoever was watching.  For sellers: a fresh comparable sale is the strongest signal to re-list or refresh. For buyers: the first hour after a visible sale is where chasing-the-spike usually starts. The cheaper opportunities are often the un-repriced comps that haven't been touched yet.  3. The first-mover holder premium  Early acquisition can become part of a piece's story. In small culture-driven collections - where holder history is visible on-chain - pieces held by early buyers sometimes carry a provenance premium when they re-list.  It's not automatic. Holders move pieces for reasons that have nothing to do with markets. But on chains where activity history is public, who held a piece and when often matters as much as which traits it has.  Quick check: open a piece's activity tab. The current owner's acquisition date is part of what you're buying.  These patterns aren't unique to any one chain. They're how thin UTXO inscription markets behave.  If you only collect on one - knowing how the others work makes you sharper on all of them.

The majority of retail investors still have no idea what to look for when it comes to dividend sustainability, and this is evident when looking at comments surrounding $PEP.  This ultimately stems from not understanding capital allocation.  As a reminder, management generally has five options for allocating free cash flow:  1. Reinvest in the existing business 2. Complete mergers and acquisitions 3. Pay down debt 4. Repurchase shares 5. Pay dividends  In other words, if a stock has a free cash flow payout ratio of 100%, then it’s using all of its capital to pay out dividends, leaving no capital to reinvest, buyback shares, or pay down debt.  So how has Pepsi’s FCF payout ratio evolved over the last few years? (see pic)  Pepsi is using all of it’s free cash flow to payout dividends.  There’s a few obvious issues with this.  For one, the company completed last year a nearly $2B acquisition of the Poppi brand.  The only way this type of move could have been made was through a weakening balance sheet, since the company could not use free cash flow to make this move.  Secondly, the company recently issued their 2026 guidance. Here’s what they said to expect:  1. Organic revenue to increase between 2 and 4 percent 2. A free cash flow conversion ratio of at least 80 percent 3. Total cash returns to shareholders of approximately $8.9 billion, comprised of dividends of $7.9 billion and share repurchases of $1.0 billion.  Let’s dissect this a bit further.  Revenue growth is not likely to be above the rate of inflation, and will most likely not come in at 4%, which is the rate they just increased their dividend. First, in most cases they have a wide moat. This means they can fend off competition, have high profit margins, strong cash flows, and can reinvest their capital at high returns.  Second: market share gains. Companies cannot always beat every competitor, which leads them to target weaker rivals and avoid stronger ones. They continuously take market share from the weaker competitors. The duopoly (or oligopoly) only strengthens further.  All of this leads them to the third, very significant long-term factor: the compound interest effect. Because they are of such high quality, incidentally gaining market share and able to reinvest their capital at high returns, investors struggle to account for the long-term effects of compounding. They are essentially cheaply valued, even if it doesn’t look that way in the present, because the compound interest effect has such a powerful influence over the long run. First, in most cases they have a wide moat. This means they can fend off competition, have high profit margins, strong cash flows, and can reinvest their capital at high returns.  Second: market share gains. Companies cannot always beat every competitor, which leads them to target weaker rivals and avoid stronger ones. They continuously take market share from the weaker competitors. The duopoly (or oligopoly) only strengthens further.  All of this leads them to the third, very significant long-term factor: the compound interest effect. Because they are of such high quality, incidentally gaining market share and able to reinvest their capital at high returns, investors struggle to account for the long-term effects of compounding. They are essentially cheaply valued, even if it doesn’t look that way in the present, because the compound interest effect has such a powerful influence over the long run.  Example of two companies with a 20-year ROIC return:  A with 18% return on capital turns $ 100 → $ 2’739 B with 6% return on capital turns $ 100 → $ 321  Quite a difference, isn’t it?

First, in most cases they have a wide moat. This means they can fend off competition, have high profit margins, strong cash flows, and can reinvest their capital at high returns.  Second: market share gains. Companies cannot always beat every competitor, which leads them to target weaker rivals and avoid stronger ones. They continuously take market share from the weaker competitors. The duopoly (or oligopoly) only strengthens further.  All of this leads them to the third, very significant long-term factor: the compound interest effect. Because they are of such high quality, incidentally gaining market share and able to reinvest their capital at high returns, investors struggle to account for the long-term effects of compounding. They are essentially cheaply valued, even if it doesn’t look that way in the present, because the compound interest effect has such a powerful influence over the long run. ✍️ Contemplating $IBRX vs $MRK  Merck’s Keytruda ($MRK) is the undisputed revenue king of oncology—a $25B+ annual juggernaut. But it relies on a biological mechanism that is fundamentally bottlenecked: taking the brakes off existing T cells. If a tumor downregulates MHC Class I (hiding from T-cell receptors) or if the patient suffers from chemotherapy-induced lymphopenia, checkpoint inhibitors hit a wall. ImmunityBio ($IBRX) is tackling this exact limitation with Anktiva (nogapendekin alfa inbakicept). Instead of just uninhibiting exhausted T cells, Anktiva acts as a IL-15 superagonist. It actively proliferates Natural Killer (NK) cells and CD8+ killer T cells to "rescue" the immune response without blowing up T-regulatory suppressive cells. In BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), Keytruda historically posted a Complete Response (CR) rate of ~19% with a median duration of response around 16 months.  Anktiva + BCG delivered a ~71% CR rate with responses extending beyond 47 months, helping over 80% of patients avoid radical cystectomy out to 3 years.  Now, ImmunityBio is using Anktiva to "rescue" Keytruda failures in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), demonstrating median overall survival of 16.2 months in checkpoint-experienced patients compared to 7–9 months historical chemotherapy benchmarks.   Why is this innovation blocked, and why does legacy chemo still control the market? Big Pharma’s moat is built on legacy standard-of-care protocols. Chemotherapy obliterates the host immune system, creating persistent lymphopenia. When checkpoint inhibitors fail in lymphopenic patients, standard oncology care defaults back to toxic chemotherapy cycles because, historically, no drug was available to rebuild the depleted immune infrastructure. Integrated GPO rebate contracts, cold-chain logistics moats, and entrenched treatment guidelines keep chemo anchored as the default backbone despite its severe toxicity. The long-term argument for NK cells over traditional chemotherapy: Chemo is a blunt weapon that destroys both healthy tissue and immune defenses. NK cells provide MHC-independent targeting—they eliminate "missing self" cancer cells that mutate to hide from T cells. This was not an isolated development. Johnson & Johnson had already taken Samsung Bioepis to court over its Stelara biosimilar launch, alleging the company breached an earlier settlement by sublicensing an additional product.  The broader governance issue is how pharmaceutical companies use litigation and secondary intellectual property rights once core patents begin to expire. Protecting legitimate innovation is important, but repeated legal challenges can also affect competition, biosimilar entry and patient access. That makes patent strategy and litigation conduct an increasingly important area of corporate accountability and regulatory scrutiny.

The government's victory in the Supreme Court also raises clear questions of corporate responisibility and good faith that Pfizer has never answered. Pendle just launched new tokenized stock markets.  You can now separate stock exposure from its dividends, starting with $NVDA and $PFE through Robinhood tokenized stocks.  How is this possible?  I looked into how Robinhood Stock Tokens work, and the interesting part is that each token accrues reinvested dividends through an onchain multiplier (tiny on NVDA, more material on names like PFE)  At a high level: PT = stock price exposure bought at a discount to 1 share-equivalent at maturity. YT = leveraged claim on multiplier growth (net reinvested dividends) until maturity  Robinhood Stock Tokens don't pay cash dividends directly to your wallet. Instead, when NVIDIA pays a dividend, Robinhood reinvests that cash into more underlying NVDA shares and increases an onchain multiplier.  So your token balance stays the same, but each token gradually represents more underlying shares. For example, Pendle currently shows:  1 NVDA token = 1.00078 NVDA shares  That extra 0.00078 represents the dividend value that has accumulated through the multiplier.  This is what @pendle_fi can split into PT and YT.  If you buy PT-NVDA, you're basically saying: “I want the NVDA exposure, but you can keep the dividends until maturity.” You buy the principal claim at a discount, then it converges toward one NVDA-share-equivalent at maturity.  That discount is what creates the fixed APY.  So if Pendle shows something like 10% fixed APY on PT-NVDA, this does NOT mean NVIDIA itself is paying a 10% dividend.  NVIDIA currently pays $0.25 per quarter, or about $1/year. At a ~$220 stock price, that's only around a 0.45% gross dividend yield.  The ~10% comes from the discount at which PT is trading relative to its maturity value.  Then there's YT, which I think is the more interesting new primitive.  YT removes the principal and gives you exposure only to the dividends generated before maturity.  And because YT costs only a fraction of the underlying stock value, your exposure to changes in that dividend stream becomes leveraged.  That starts looking much closer to an onchain dividend derivative than simply another way to trade tokenized stocks.  And this is where I think the bigger opportunity appears:  Pendle can potentially become an onchain market for dividend expectations.  Instead of only asking: “Will NVDA go up?” you can now separately express a view on: “How valuable will NVDA's dividends be over the next few months?”  And once stocks become composable like this, dividends are probably only the beginning.  Principal can become one market. Dividends can become another.  Pendle letting people trade PT/YT on $NVDA and $PFE might look like a small market launch today. That makes patent strategy and litigation conduct an increasingly important area of corporate accountability and regulatory scrutiny.

Tau + RNA Tissue Expression for Key Drug Targets in Atopic Dermatitis  $CRVS #ITK - High Tau 0.88 $SNY $REGN IL-4Rα - Low/Med Tau 0.27 $KYMR #STAT6 - Low Tau 0.16 $ABBV #JAK1 - Low Tau 0.15  Based on research and Tau for oral drugs in development for AD: $CRVS ITK inhibitor soquelitinib $KYMR STAT6 degrader KT-621 may have implications for safety  Low Tau for STAT6, like JAK1 and IL-4Rα does not alone predict toxicity, but does indicate larger number of tissues and organs could potentially be affected. Safety comes from combination of pathway breadth, genetics, tissue-specific phenotypes, drug distribution, etc.  High ITK Tau predicts fewer direct organ systems at risk, but potentially a concentrated immune/lymphoid AE profile.  ITK high tau should mean soqueltinib would have a narrower and more predictable on-target safety footprint than STAT6 w/ low tau targeted by KT-621.  ITK’s strongest advantage is that the target is largely confined to lymphoid and T-cell biology (see image comparing to JAK1, IL-4Rα, and STAT6). This predicts a narrow immune-functional safety profile to monitor  Whereas STAT6 in expressed in most tissues, however, STAT6 occupies a narrower signalling position than JAK1 despite having a similar tau number, but is more broadly expressed than ITK and has functions extending beyond simple IL-4/IL-13 receptor signalling. So while, KT-621 may achieve broader and more uniform suppression of type-2 biology, near-complete STAT6 degradation carries a larger unknown pleiotropy risk that has the potential to affect multiple tissues/organs, especially involving macrophages, metabolic liver biology, and helminth protection and tissue responses that are not replicated by IL-4Rα blockade.  This may require a broad profile of tissues and organs to monitor beyond immune functions.  Summary comparison ITK: best immune-cell restriction, but complete inbibition may pose infection risk IL-4Rα: best overall target de-risking despite low Tau and now years of #duplimab safety data have proven drug and target to be low risk STAT6: complete degradation carries in light of its very low tau opens up possible pleiotropic risk across multiple organs and tissues that may not be predictable from IL-4Rα biology JAK1: strongest combination of broad expression, network centrality and LoF constraint; highest inherent on-target safety burden which has been observed in the drug #upadacitinib and its black box warning  Tau is just ONE number to consider when evaluating drug targets and potential safety risks, but has shown correlations in literature. Importantly for KT-621, research supports concern about potential systemic tissue exposure, but Tau alone cannot quantify the consequences of near-complete STAT6 degradation.    Ongoing Ph2b trials for Corvus ITK inhibitor soquelitinib and Kymera STAT6 degrader KT-621 will be very insightful regarding the safety of these developing oral therapies in atopic dermatitis and I look forward to the upcoming data

Eventually, expectations will have to be reconciled with reality — either Novo’s valuation rises, or the market’s expectations for more highly valued peers come down.  I find it difficult to believe Novo will remain priced like this indefinitely. Whether the gap closes in weeks, months or years is another question entirely. 7-15-26 What Bonds Know That Stocks Don't $TLT $BND  Yesterday's CPI grabbed the headlines, but the #bondmarket barely reacted. Treasury yields ended up almost exactly where they were before the inflation report, suggesting the market had already priced in the broader economic outlook.  The key takeaway is that if you want to understand where inflation and interest rates are headed, don't just watch monthly CPI reports. Watch wage growth.  Wages, inflation, economic growth, and interest rates are all connected, and the bond market continuously prices those expectations into Treasury #yields.  A 10-year Treasury yield reflects much more than inflation. It compensates investors for expected inflation, opportunity cost, credit risk, and a small market risk premium. That's why yields often provide a clearer picture of the economy than a single data release.  Short-term events can still move yields. Rising oil prices, geopolitical tensions, Fed expectations, and economic surprises all influence bond markets. If #crudeoil climbs back toward $80–90 per barrel, investors may demand higher yields to compensate for renewed inflation risks.  For long-term investors, however, the focus should be on structural trends rather than daily headlines.  America's $39 trillion debt burden is likely to slow economic growth and productivity over time, ultimately putting downward pressure on both growth and inflation. If that outlook proves correct, today's Treasury yields may be attractive levels to lock in for investors seeking capital preservation and portfolio stability.  The bond market isn't reacting to yesterday's CPI because it's looking years ahead. That's what bonds know that stocks often don't. 8-31-26 Own Bonds? Here’s Where You Want To Be On The Yield Curve $TLT $BND  There’s an interesting contradiction developing in the bond market. Kevin Warsh has argued that the Fed needs to get out of the business of driving financial markets. Bonds should trade on inflation, growth, credit conditions and supply/demand. Stocks should trade on earnings and fundamentals.  The Fed shouldn’t be the signal. It should take its signal from the markets.  That would be a major shift from the last 15 years, when virtually every market correction immediately became about the Fed: Will it cut rates? Will it launch QE? What will it do to support markets?  But just as Warsh wants the Fed to step back, the Treasury is stepping in.  Treasury buyback operations could support the long end of the curve and potentially suppress longer-term yields. That means another policy variable is influencing bond prices at exactly the moment Warsh wants markets to rediscover genuine price discovery. For investors, that makes the long end particularly complicated.  Treasury buybacks could push yields lower, but several forces are pulling in the opposite direction. Higher #crudeoil prices are increasing inflation concerns. Tariffs could add more inflationary pressure. There’s also significant positioning around the Treasury basis trade and heavy short exposure against bonds, creating the potential for sharp moves in either direction.  So simply buying long-duration Treasuries because Treasury may provide a bid isn’t necessarily the best strategy. Instead, consider focusing more of your fixed-income exposure on the short end and belly of the curve.  The 1–3 year area can offer attractive #yields with less duration risk, while the 3–5 and 5–7 year areas provide a middle ground for investors who want to lock in yields without taking excessive long-end volatility. If inflation is the main concern, TIPS can also play a role. That doesn’t mean avoiding long-duration Treasuries completely.  Today’s yields could ultimately prove attractive if inflation and economic growth cool and rates eventually move lower. Some longer-duration exposure may therefore make sense, but it doesn’t need to be a large position.  The point isn’t to perfectly predict where the 10-year or 30-year yield goes next. With Treasury intervention, inflation, oil, tariffs, basis trades and heavy short positioning all pulling on bonds simultaneously, this may be an environment where diversifying across the yield curve makes more sense than making one huge bet on the long end. But Lacy Hunt argues that era may be over. His thesis is based on the Fisher equation, which says long-term Treasury yields are driven by three components: real interest rates, inflation expectations, and the risk (or term) premium. According to Dr Hunt, all three are now pointing higher.   *   First, real interest rates are likely to rise as the economy enters a period of capital scarcity. Unlike the past several decades of abundant savings and inexpensive financing, capital is becoming more valuable, pushing borrowing costs higher.  Second, inflation expectations are shifting upward. Dr Hunt believes the low-inflation environment that defined roughly 1990–2020 is ending. Instead of inflation averaging around 1.5%–2.5%, he expects it to gradually settle into a higher long-term range of approximately 3.5%–4.5%.  Structural inflation pressures are becoming more persistent, making higher inflation the new baseline rather than a temporary spike.  The third factor is the most overlooked: the risk premium. Investors have historically treated U.S. Treasuries as nearly risk-free, but Dr Hunt argues that worsening fiscal conditions will force investors to demand greater compensation for holding long-term government debt.   *   A major concern is the rapid rise in government interest expense. Citing economic historian Niall Ferguson, Dr Hunt notes that great powers often begin to decline when interest payments on government debt exceed military spending.    He goes even further, arguing that rising interest costs don't just reflect fiscal deterioration—they contribute to even higher future borrowing costs by increasing investor concerns about long-term fiscal sustainability.  Dr Hunt also expects the coming investment environment to look very different from the relatively calm period between 1990 and 2020. Markets are likely to become much more volatile, and that volatility itself will push investors to demand an even larger term premium, reinforcing higher long-term yields.  *  That doesn't mean interest rates will rise in a straight line. Recessions, slower monetary growth, tighter monetary policy, or favorable supply shocks could temporarily push rates lower. However, Dr Hunt sees those as cyclical interruptions within a broader structural trend toward higher inflation and higher yields.  Because rising yields are negative for bond prices, he is positioning defensively. Higher real rates, higher inflation expectations, and higher risk premiums suggest that long-term Treasury yields are likely to trend higher for years, even if the path is volatile. 8-28-26 The Bond Market Is Setting Up For A Massive Short Squeeze $TLT $BND  The bond market may be building one of its most interesting contrarian setups — not simply because inflation and wage growth are declining, but because positioning has become extremely stretched.  There is currently a massive short position against Treasury bonds, much of it tied to leveraged hedge funds running the basis trade. These funds attempt to capture small pricing differences between Treasury securities and futures, often using significant leverage and short Treasury futures as a hedge.  That creates the potential for a powerful unwind. If an event causes Treasury yields to drop sharply, those leveraged short positions could come under pressure. Hedge funds would then be forced to cover their shorts, which means buying bonds.  That could create a self-reinforcing cycle: yields fall sharply → bond prices rise → Treasury shorts come under pressure → hedge funds cover → bond prices rise further → yields fall even more → additional shorts are forced to cover.  Goldman Sachs has highlighted similar dynamics in its conditional projections for the 10-year and 30-year Treasury markets.  This is why the bond opportunity right now isn't necessarily about making a long-term call that yields have peaked forever. It's about positioning, leverage and the potential mechanics of forced short covering.  Bonds are already extremely stretched to the downside. If the basis trade begins to unwind, there could be substantial upside in Treasuries as shorts rush to cover.  But there is an important catch: this needs a catalyst. If yields simply drift gradually lower, it may not create enough pressure to force hedge funds out of their positions. The market likely needs an event that causes yields to fall sharply enough to trigger the initial wave of short covering.  Once that happens, leverage could amplify the move dramatically.  So the setup is there, but patience matters. This isn't necessarily a trade that happens tomorrow.  The key is watching for a sharp move lower in yields that begins forcing leveraged Treasury shorts to unwind. Funds like $BND, $BNDX, and $TLT were originally created to give investors easy, diversified exposure to the bond market.  But they have one major flaw:  They never mature.  When the bonds inside these ETFs approach maturity, the funds sell or replace them with new bonds.  That means investors remain permanently exposed to changes in interest rates, with no guaranteed price at which their principal will be returned.  Individual bonds work differently.  If you purchase a high-quality bond and hold it until maturity, temporary price fluctuations become far less important. Assuming the issuer does not default, you receive the bond’s face value when it matures.  With a traditional bond ETF, there is no maturity date to anchor the investment.  This became painfully clear in 2021 and 2022.  But Bond ETFs do offer several important advantages over buying individual bonds.  First, bond ETFs provide instant diversification.  Instead of relying on a single company or government issuer, investors can own hundreds or even thousands of bonds through one fund. This reduces the damage that a single default could have on the portfolio.  Second, bond ETFs are highly liquid.  Individual bonds can sometimes be difficult to buy or sell, and pricing is not always transparent. Bond ETFs trade throughout the day just like stocks, making it much easier to enter or exit a position.  Third, they are significantly more convenient.  Building and maintaining a diversified bond portfolio requires researching issuers, monitoring maturity dates, reinvesting principal, and managing interest payments.  A bond ETF handles all of this automatically.  Bond ETFs also make it easier to target a specific type of exposure.  Investors can choose funds based on:  • Maturity and duration • Credit quality • Government or corporate debt • Municipal bonds • High-yield bonds • Domestic or international exposure  They can also be useful for investors who want consistent monthly income without having to build and maintain their own bond ladder.  And while traditional bond ETFs never mature, defined-maturity bond ETFs provide a useful middle ground.  These funds hold diversified portfolios of bonds that mature around a specific year, allowing investors to combine the diversification and convenience of an ETF with a more predictable timeline for the return of their capital.  So, the argument is not that investors should never own bond ETFs.  The argument is that investors must understand what they are buying.  A traditional bond ETF is not simply a diversified version of an individual bond-  It is a perpetual portfolio with ongoing interest-rate exposure.  For investors who prioritize liquidity, diversification, simplicity, and monthly income, bond ETFs can be a phenomenal option.

The $CVS suit against Tennessee's PBM ownership ban is not just a fight over vertical integration, it's a fight over the drug-pricing machine itself. PBMs sit between manufacturers and patients, shape which drugs get covered, steer volume through affiliated channels, and still leave patients paying more through a maze of rebates, markups, and opaque incentives.  The core argument for separation is that the same firms should not control formularies, reimbursement, and pharmacy ownership while claiming to lower costs for everyone else.  If the system rewards opacity, scale, and hidden extraction, patients should not be surprised that they keep paying more.  The conflict of interest is real, even if some Medicare data complicates the simplest price-harm claim. The broader patient complaint is about opacity, leverage, and a system that can preserve higher costs without clearly showing who benefits.

One name that stands above the rest to me is $MAIN   Main Street Capital isn’t a REIT—it’s an internally managed Business Development Company (BDC) with roughly a $5.2B market cap that lends to and invests in lower middle-market businesses.  Why I like it:  • Monthly dividends (currently $0.265/share) • Monthly dividend increased 1.9% sequentially and 3.9% YoY • Regular supplemental dividends when portfolio exits generate excess gains (recently $0.30/share) • Forward dividend yield around 5.7-8% depending on supplemental payouts • Dividend payout ratio around 78% of core earnings • Net Investment Income (NII) has consistently covered the dividend by 100%+ • Never cut its regular dividend since its 2007 IPO • Over $50/share in cumulative dividends paid since inception • Lower beta of roughly 0.70, providing some downside protection • Internally managed structure keeps fees low, reduces expense drag, and aligns management with shareholders  The business model is simple.  $MAIN provides customized one-stop financing through senior secured debt, subordinated debt, and equity investments in private companies with roughly $10M-$150M in revenue (while its private loan platform reaches companies up to $500M in revenue).  The debt generates recurring interest income.  The equity investments—often 5-50% ownership stakes—create upside that helps fund supplemental dividends.  That’s a powerful combination.  The company has investments across roughly 178 portfolio companies, manages approximately $9.2B of capital, maintains diversified exposure across multiple industries, and emphasizes conservative underwriting with historically low non-accruals.  Profitability has remained impressive with roughly 14% ROE, ~75% profit margins, and 16 consecutive quarters of NAV growth.  Preliminary Q2 2026 results showed NAV climbing again to approximately $33.88-$33.96, up 1.2-1.5% QoQ, even after paying its recent supplemental dividend.  The biggest risk?  Quality isn’t cheap.  With NAV around $33.9 and shares trading near $55, investors are paying roughly a 1.6x price-to-NAV premium for one of the best dividend track records in the BDC industry.   If credit markets weaken, defaults increase, or lending spreads tighten, that premium could compress.  Ironically, that premium also benefits shareholders because $MAIN can issue equity above NAV, making new capital raises accretive and helping fund future investments. The Kroger Co. NYSE: $KR  One thing I watch in retail is how companies connect the weekly shopping trip with the rest of a customer's routine. Kroger's September 30 card launch makes that connection quite explicit.  The Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard links rewards to customers' loyalty accounts. Its published structure includes up to 5X Points through Kroger's website and app, 4X at participating Kroger fuel pumps and up to 3X in stores, subject to program terms.  Imprint powers the technology, with applications and rewards management available through Kroger's app or website. The offer also includes a complimentary Boost Essential membership, with delivery benefits subject to minimum-purchase requirements.  From a business perspective, the interesting detail is the joined-up experience: shopping, fuel, loyalty and account management in the same customer ecosystem. That's a concrete product rollout to watch for engagement, rather than evidence of a sales increase already achieved. Faster-moving institutions can underwrite new products earlier.
